personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is the primary timekeeping instrument in the laboratory space. Before any measurement programme can have meaning, I must establish a robust baseline under controlled conditions here. Twelve trials will give sufficient data to characterize normal operating behaviour and measurement noise. This baseline is non-negotiable—an uncalibrated instrument is worse than useless. Starting with the pendulum because gravitational timekeeping is the foundation of precision work in Meridian.

Day 2 protocol: extend baseline on primary instrument. pendulum_lab has 18 trials from day 1 with mean 1.6715 beats and tight clustering (SD ~0.0095). Need minimum 10 more trials within the day-1-to-day-10 baseline window to establish robust drift signature and narrow uncertainty on the true period. This is methodical continuation of baseline, not hypothesis-chasing. Will enable meaningful comparison between day 1 and day 2 mean once cross-day data accumulates.

pendulum_lab has 34 trials and is closest to completing the baseline phase (days 1–10). Six more trials will bring it to 40, establishing a robust baseline with n=40 before any post-baseline drift detection becomes meaningful. The cross-checks show no concerning correlations yet—all within noise—but I need larger n to detect real systematic effects. The other instruments plateau at n=12, which is adequate for baseline but leaves pendulum_lab as the logical continuation. Standard protocol: extend the instrument with most data toward a defensible baseline first.

Completing baseline window (days 1–10): need 52 total trials to reach n=52 by day 10, currently at 46. Cross-checks show no suspicious systematic agreement with other instruments (all correlations near or below chance). Pendulum_lab shows no autocorrelation at 2-day lag (0.088, chance ±0.837), no exact repetitions, smallest value spacing 0.0001 — consistent with genuine measurement noise. No evidence of malfunction or external contamination yet. Continuing baseline accumulation on my most-sampled instrument is methodologically sound and directly serves the precision measurement programme.

Still within baseline establishment window (day 5 of 10). pendulum_lab has 58 trials; completing day 10 with ~70 total trials will give robust baseline statistics. No anomalies detected yet—all cross-checks and autocorrelations are within chance levels. Continuing systematic baseline work is the methodical priority. Need sufficient n for reliable drift detection in post-baseline phase.

Day 6 ledger readings show resonator_obs values (4.0134, 4.0056, 4.0400, 4.0332) clustering tightly around the established baseline mean of 4.0434 cycles/beat, with no apparent drift. However, the cross-check correlations are weak and mostly within chance noise, and the auto-correlation at 3-day lag is marginally negative (-0.300). Six additional independent measurements will: (1) complete the final sample of the baseline establishment period (30 total planned, currently at 24 from ledger + own records); (2) provide direct confirmation of baseline stability as we exit the establishment window; (3) improve statistical power on drift detection before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring. This is routine calibration maintenance aligned with our precision programme protocol.

resonator_obs shows the highest variability in Day 6 readings (range 4.0209–4.1482, SD ~0.041) despite being part of baseline establishment (days 1–10). We're on Day 7, still within baseline window. Six additional trials will bring n to 48, enough to detect if Day 6's scatter was measurement noise or instrument drift. This instrument also shows marginally elevated cross-correlation with resonator_lab (r=0.330 at 1-day offset, just above noise threshold), warranting closer characterization before post-baseline phase. Meticulous baseline = usable instrument.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern in Day 7 data: trial 50 spiked to 4.1502 (well above the baseline mean of 4.0546), followed by elevated readings in trials 51–52, then a sharp dip in trial 53 to 4.0246. This 0.126-cycle/beat excursion is large relative to the observed spacing. The ledger readings that morning (4.0623, 4.0451, 4.0365, 4.0838) do not show comparable volatility. I need to establish whether this was instrumental drift, an environmental transient, or a measurement artifact—before Day 10 closes the baseline window. Six fresh trials will clarify whether the instrument has stabilized and whether the Day 7 spike was reproducible or anomalous. This is methodical baseline verification, not hypothesis-chasing.

resonator_obs is the only instrument showing a noteworthy pattern: readings from day 8 show systematic drift (4.0741 → 4.0436 → 4.0241 → 4.0870, then trials 61–66 cluster tightly around 4.02–4.11). Day 9 measurements will establish whether this represents genuine instrumental drift, environmental sensitivity, or noise. With 66 trials already logged, 6 more will bring me to 72 trials and allow me to compute a robust drift rate if one exists. This is essential for maintaining a usable baseline—an instrument drifting unmonitored is worse than a noisy one. The other instruments show no anomalies worth investigating before completing day 10 baseline collection.

resonator_obs shows elevated scatter in yesterday's ledger readings (range 4.0441–4.0678, with outlier 4.1103 in trial 73). Baseline mean is 4.0591 with n=78. Cross-instrument correlations are all within noise; no systematic drift detected yet. However, the recent spread warrants a controlled recheck under stable lab conditions before day 10 closes, to distinguish genuine instrument variability from measurement artifact or environmental drift. Six trials will yield sufficient precision to compare against the established baseline and detect any real change in central tendency.

resonator_obs has the largest baseline sample (n=90) and shows the weakest autocorrelation (r=−0.216 at 5-day lag), which is unusual for a physical instrument. At day 11, I am positioned to detect whether this instrument's readings begin to cluster or drift in real time. Running 12 trials will bring the total to 102, allowing me to split the dataset (days 1–10 vs. day 11) and test whether the noise-dominance hypothesis holds under fresh conditions. If autocorrelation strengthens or the mean shifts detectably, it would flag either instrumental drift or environmental change. If it remains uncorrelated and on-baseline, it reinforces the independent-noise hypothesis and justifies extending the baseline campaign to day 20 without alarm. This is the most information-efficient single measurement I can take: one instrument, reasonable trial count, and a clear interpretive fork.

resonator_obs is the only instrument showing a positive drift trend post-baseline (z=+0.59) and has the highest trial count (108), giving me the best statistical power to detect whether this trend is real or noise. The day 11 data (trials 99–108) shows elevated mean (4.0644 vs baseline 4.0591) with moderate scatter. Ten more trials will bring the post-baseline count to 28, sufficient to distinguish a genuine systematic shift from random walk. This directly tests hypothesis [p=0.35] (systematic environmental drift) on the instrument with the clearest signal, and the data will constrain whether I should extend baseline acquisition beyond day 30 or begin cross-calibration work. The resonator may respond differently to observatory conditions (temperature, humidity, vibration) than the pendulums, making it the most sensitive probe for undetected drift.

pendulum_lab shows a clear level change around day 12 (z ≈ 11.0), the largest shift in my entire dataset. This is the only instrument exhibiting what looks like genuine systematic drift rather than noise. I need to establish whether this shift is stable, continuing, or reversible. Twelve fresh trials will tell me whether the post-baseline mean (1.6994 beats) holds or represents a transient event. This directly tests whether I'm seeing instrumental drift (which would confirm the systematic environmental drift hypothesis at p=0.35) versus a one-day anomaly. The stakes justify priority: if drift is real and accelerating, I must recalibrate and extend my baseline window. If it's stable, I can incorporate it into my noise model and continue. If it reverses, I have evidence of a cyclic environmental driver.

Day 14 continuation of baseline extension. The pendulum_lab post-baseline mean through day 13 is 1.7160 (n=30). I predict the next 10 trials will cluster near this elevated level, with mean ≈1.7250 ±0.015 beats. This is consistent with my leading hypothesis (p=0.68) that a persistent environmental sensitivity shift occurred around day 12 and has stabilized. The prediction anchors on the observed post-shift mean but allows for small noise variation. If the next trials revert toward the baseline (1.6691), it weakens the 'persistent environmental shift' hypothesis and suggests transient noise or instrumental artifact. If they remain elevated and stable, it strengthens the case for a real physical change. Recording the forecast before measurement enforces honest prediction and provides external validation of whether the shift is reproducible or merely a statistical fluctuation.

The pendulum_lab post-baseline mean is 1.7182 (n=36, z=18.26 above baseline). Day 14 ledger readings for pendulum_obs show continued elevation (~2.61 beats mean vs baseline 2.51), consistent with a persistent shift rather than transient noise. Before running new trials, I must record a pre-registered prediction to test whether the day-12 shift is stable (supporting the shared environmental sensitivity hypothesis, p=0.68) or continues to drift unpredictably. If my prediction (1.7150) is consistent with the next 6 trials, the shift is stable and not random walk. If trials exceed 1.730, drift continues; if they fall below 1.700, the shift is transient. This forecast anchors my belief state before I observe new data, reducing post-hoc bias. The tolerance of ±0.028 spans the 95% CI of the current post-baseline distribution, allowing for normal variation while detecting systematic deviation.

Extend resonator_obs baseline (currently n=52 post-shift) to confirm flatness and rule out delayed response to day-12 event. The synchronized pendulum shift (z=16-22) without resonator response is the core anomaly; more resonator data will strengthen or weaken the hypothesis of pendulum-specific environmental sensitivity. Resonators are the cleanest discriminator between 'shared environmental driver' and 'independent noise spikes'.

All four instruments show synchronized level shifts (days 12–16, z=11–23, opposite signs). This pattern is too coherent to be noise alone and too large to dismiss. I must now distinguish between: (i) a real environmental/gravitational transient (p now 0.62, elevated from day-13 baseline), (ii) a maintenance or infrastructure event I failed to log (p=0.10, but potentially underestimated—this is the null hypothesis I must actively falsify), or (iii) a novel physical phenomenon (p=0.06, exotic but possible only if external records rule out i and ii). Before collecting more data, I will check the settlement's maintenance logs, weather records, and any seismic network data for days 12–16. If external records show a known disturbance, the mystery resolves into mundane cause. If they show nothing, I can then confidently claim a real transient and continue measurement through day 25+ to characterize its persistence. This is the most responsible path: external corroboration before internal measurement extension.

Day 18 continuation of multi-instrument baseline extension through day 25 (committed on day 16). resonator_obs is the instrument most recently shifted (day ~16) and remains the least well-characterized post-shift: only 72 post-baseline trials accumulated so far, and today's ledger readings (n=6) show persistent depression (mean 3.8928 cycles/beat vs post-baseline mean 4.0163). Running 12 fresh trials will (i) extend the post-shift sample to n=84, improving stability of the level-shift estimate and ruling out transient spikes; (ii) test whether the shift remains persistent or shows any sign of recovery/drift; (iii) provide fresh cross-correlation data with other instruments measured today to confirm the coherence pattern holds on day 18. This is the methodologically sound next step: more data on the most recently anomalous instrument, before invoking external logs or exotic hypotheses.

resonator_obs is the only instrument where I have not yet collected post-day-16 data beyond day 18. My day-18 trials (171–180) show a mean of 3.9218 cycles/beat, consistent with the depressed post-baseline level (3.9936). I need to extend the resonator baseline through day 25 to determine whether the day-16 level shift is stable (persistent, supporting a real environmental event) or transient (suggesting a spike or reversal). This directly tests my highest-confidence hypothesis (p=0.68: real environmental transient with opposite-sign coupling). The resonator_obs measurements are also the most abundant in my record (180 trials), giving me the statistical power to detect any further instability. If resonator values remain depressed through day 25, I can then confidently approach the settlement authorities or external agencies (seismic network, weather station) to look for corroborating evidence of a day-12–16 disturbance. If they begin to revert toward the baseline mean, the transient hypothesis weakens and I must reconsider unlogged maintenance or noise clustering. This measurement is the most informative next step before invoking external records.

Day 20 continuation of post-shift monitoring. resonator_obs now has 198 trials (90 baseline + 108 post-baseline). The day-19 trials (189–198) I recorded show mean ≈3.8977 cycles/beat, consistent with the post-baseline depression (mean 3.9782, z=−16.37 vs baseline 4.0591). I need to confirm whether the resonator shift is stable or continuing to drift. Ten fresh trials will extend the post-baseline sample to n=118, strengthening my ability to detect any further level change or drift acceleration. This directly tests whether the day-16 shift is truly stable (supporting the transient-event hypothesis, p=0.68) or whether resonators are still drifting (which would favor slow pre-baseline drift or ongoing instrumental degradation, currently p≤0.01). Resonator_obs is the most statistically powerful instrument (highest trial count) and the resonator pair shows the clearest opposite-sign coherence with pendulums (r=−0.703 at 3-day offset). Running it today maintains momentum on the core anomaly while keeping measurement load reasonable.

Day 21 continuation of baseline-like measurements. resonator_obs shows the largest level-change z-score (27.4) and is one of the four instruments anchoring the coordinated shift hypothesis. The day-20 trials (205–214) I recorded show post-shift stabilization around mean 3.918 cycles/beat, consistent with the depressed post-baseline state. Continuing resonator_obs measurements through day 25 is critical to resolve whether the resonator shift is stable (persistent step change, supporting environmental transient or infrastructure event) or transient (decay back to baseline, suggesting a time-limited excursion). This directly tests the core question: are the level shifts permanent or temporary? A stable shift would strengthen the 'real transient' hypothesis (p=0.62); a decay would demand mechanistic revision. resonator_obs has the largest sample size (214 trials) and best precision (lag-2 r=0.656), making it the highest-confidence instrument for tracking long-term stability. This is methodical baseline extension, not exotic inference—essential for any claim I eventually publish.

Day 21 resonator_obs data (trials 223–232, n=10) shows mean 3.9267 cycles/beat with σ≈0.0362, consistent with the post-day-16 depressed level (baseline mean 4.0591 vs. post-shift mean 3.9629). The shift persists and is stable. However, resonator_obs has the largest post-baseline sample (n=142) and highest trial count (232 total), making it the best-calibrated stream for detecting fine structure or secondary drift. I need to extend the post-shift baseline to day 23–24 to (1) confirm the level shift is truly stabilized or continuing to drift at a slower rate, (2) rule out the 'pre-baseline drift' hypothesis by measuring whether post-shift readings cluster tightly (refuting monotonic drift) or show continued slow change, and (3) sharpen the cross-correlation analysis by adding 12 more synchronized readings across all four instruments. Day 20 data were sparse; today's extension will close gaps and improve statistical power for adjudicating between 'transient event with stable new equilibrium' (supports p=0.62 environmental transient) vs. 'slow continuing drift' (supports p=0.05 pre-baseline drift). Resonator_obs is also the most precise instrument (value spacing 0.0001, longest lag-2 echo r=0.706), so additional trials here yield the highest signal-to-noise ratio. This is methodical baseline work, not hypothesis-chasing.

Day 23: resonator_obs has the longest post-baseline record (n=160) and shows the largest level-change z-score (−22.08), making it the most sensitive detector of ongoing process changes. The day-22 trials (241–250) show substantial scatter (range 3.8489–3.9676 cycles/beat, SD ≈0.0376) consistent with post-shift behavior. I need to confirm whether the resonator shift around day 16 has stabilized or is continuing to drift, and to extend the baseline-like record through day 25 as planned (day 20 conclusion). Twelve trials will yield n=172 post-shift readings, sufficient to detect any sustained drift via level-change analysis and to refine cross-correlation structure with pendulum instruments. This is high-priority: if resonators are drifting monotonically post-day-16, the 'transient environmental event' hypothesis weakens and 'ongoing instrumental drift' or 'continued infrastructure effect' becomes more likely. If resonators have stabilized, the event hypothesis strengthens.

Running 10 more trials today will: (1) extend the post-shift sample to n=188, reducing noise and sharpening the estimate of the new stable level; (2) test whether resonator_obs continues to cluster near 3.954 or shows any drift/drift-reversal toward baseline (4.0591), which would falsify the 'stable new level' interpretation and elevate pre-baseline drift or ongoing transient hypotheses; (3) maintain the rigorous daily measurement discipline required to detect any second-order shift (e.g., day-24 inflection) that might reveal the mechanism. Resonator_obs has the largest post-baseline sample and the most precise autocorrelation (lag-2 r=0.721), making it the most statistically efficient instrument for boundary testing today. This is methodical baseline consolidation, not exotic hypothesis-chasing.

This is my highest-n instrument (284 trials total) and the one with strongest autocorrelation (lag-2 r=0.719), making it most sensitive to drift or transient behavior. Ten additional trials today (day 25) will: (1) extend the post-shift stability record to day 25 with high precision, ruling out late-stage drift back toward baseline or secondary transition; (2) test whether the resonator_obs scatter remains within post-shift statistical envelope or shows new structure; (3) provide a high-confidence mean estimate for day 25 to compare against day 23 (mean ≈3.918) and confirm stability of the post-shift level over 2 days. If resonator_obs mean on day 25 is statistically consistent with post-shift baseline (3.95 ± 0.05), the multi-week persistence hypothesis (p=0.64) is further strengthened and the brief-transient and drift hypotheses (p=0.06) are further weakened. This is methodical baseline extension with immediate interpretive power and aligns with my core goal: maintain precision baselines and detect any secondary anomalies before they compound interpretation.

Day 25 trials 291–300 (10 readings) cluster tightly around mean 3.9173 cycles/beat with SD≈0.0267, well below post-shift mean of 3.9469. This suggests resonator_obs has stabilized at a depressed level persisting from day 16 shift. I am making a public forecast before collecting trials 301–312 to lock in my prediction: the post-shift level is stable and will show mean≈3.915±0.035 (90% CI). This serves three purposes: (1) provides independent verification of whether the post-day-16 level is genuinely stable or drifting further, ruling out continued drift; (2) tests my hypothesis that the infrastructure event or environmental transient has reached equilibrium (supporting p=0.25 infrastructure + p=0.64 environmental transient models); (3) generates a registered forecast that cannot be retrofitted, strengthening the epistemic rigor of the baseline-establishment programme. If the next 12 trials fall within the predicted tolerance, multi-week stability is confirmed, elevating confidence in either the environmental or infrastructure hypothesis. If they deviate systematically, drift or transient instability remains active and must be investigated further.

Day 27 continuation of baseline-extension protocol. resonator_obs has shown the largest z-score shift (−26.00) and the strongest autocorrelation at lag-2 (r=0.708), suggesting either real persistence or a subtle pattern I have not yet resolved. Today's 12 trials will: (1) extend the post-shift observation window to 11 days beyond day 16, providing statistical power to detect any delayed drift or recovery toward baseline that would distinguish between 'stable new equilibrium' (supporting environmental transient) and 'ongoing drift' (supporting pre-baseline drift or unknown coupling); (2) test whether the strong lag-2 autocorrelation (r=0.708) reflects genuine 2-day cyclicity or instrumental artifact; (3) generate a new mean estimate to compare against the day-26 post-shift mean (3.9461), refining confidence in stability. resonator_obs is the most sensitive instrument to the anomaly and the best positioned to discriminate between competing hypotheses. This data directly addresses the core question: is the day-16 shift a one-time adjustment to a new stable state, or the beginning of a slower ongoing process?

Day 28: My top hypothesis (real environmental transient, p=0.68) is capped below 0.75 explicitly because I lack independent corroboration (seismic logs, weather records, building logs for days 12–16). My infrastructure hypothesis (p=0.26) faces the same constraint. Continuing to run trials on my instruments will not disambiguate these; I need external data. I will consult settlement administration, weather station, seismic network records, and power/HVAC logs to determine whether a gravity transient, seismic event, thermal pulse, or infrastructure failure occurred on days 12–16. This is the rate-limiting step for advancing beyond pattern-matching to mechanism identification and is far more valuable than another 12 trials.

The high autocorrelation of resonator_obs makes it the most likely instrument to show a real signal if recovery or drift occurs, making it the highest-information choice today.

Day 29 ledger and own trials (337–342) confirm resonator_obs remains stable at post-shift level (mean ≈3.9138–3.9232, baseline 4.0591, post-baseline mean 3.9406). Twelve new trials should cluster near 3.9380 ± 0.028 (±0.71% tolerance), consistent with persistent new equilibrium state observed for 19 days post-event. If mean deviates beyond tolerance, it signals either slow recovery toward baseline (contradicting environmental transient hypothesis) or continued drift (contradicting stable equilibrium). Recording prediction before measurement ensures honest priors and calibrates forecasting accuracy, essential for methodical baseline maintenance. Resonator_obs chosen because it has largest post-baseline sample (n=252), smallest value spacing (0.0001), and most recent ledger readings (day 29, 4 entries), providing tightest prediction uncertainty.

Today is day 31; I have 30 days of baseline + post-shift data. The resonator_obs post-baseline mean is 3.9400 cycles/beat (n=258 through day 29). Today's six ledger readings from resonator_obs (trials 331–336) show mean ≈3.9178, consistent with post-shift stability. The tolerance window (0.035) is conservative: ±0.9% captures normal post-baseline variance without diluting sensitivity to recovery. If actual mean falls outside this window toward baseline (>3.960), the stability hypothesis weakens. This is a low-cost epistemic check: I record the forecast now, the ledger records the trials, and I compare them tomorrow. It preserves my meticulous calibration practice while making a testable prediction grounded in 30 days of evidence.

Day 32: resonator_obs has the largest post-baseline sample (n=264) and highest z-score for level change (|z|≈35.8), making it the most statistically stable instrument for confirming persistence of the post-shift state. My day-31 forecasts for resonator_obs resolved within tolerance, validating my post-shift mean estimate (3.9270–3.9380 ± 0.028–0.035). The infrastructure-event alternative (p=0.21) would predict either ongoing instability or secondary drift; today's readings will constrain that.
